s.d: (derogatory) One with no religious beliefs.

s.d: the quality of being unfaithful

(uncountable) Unfaithfulness in a marriage or an intimate (sexual or romantic) relationship: practice or instance of having a sexual or romantic affair with someone other than one's spouse, without the consent of the spouse.
x: Your friends tell you rumors about your girlfriend's infidelity or you remember being broken up around the time the baby was conceived.

s.d: (uncountable) Unfaithfulness in some other moral obligation.
(archaic, uncountable) Lack of religious belief.
x: The Churchman remarked that such incidents arose from the growing infidelity, while the Freethinker saw in them a reversion to superstition.

boxing at close quarters
(uncountable) Fighting or quarreling among the members of a single group or side.

infiltrate.e: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

s.d: Any undesirable substance or group of cells that has made its way into part of the body.
x: One critical distinction to make is whether a focal corneal infiltrate is infected with bacteria or is a sterile immunologic response.
Extensive lumpy infiltrates with a tendency to caseate and to form fistulas with purulent secretions appear, mainly in the anogenital region.

s.d: cause (a liquid) to enter by penetrating the interstices
enter a group or organization in order to spy on the members
x: The student organization was infiltrated by a traitor

s.d: pass into or through by filtering or permeating
x: the substance infiltrated the material

s.d: pass through an enemy line; in a military conflict
To surreptitiously penetrate, enter or gain access to.
x: The spy infiltrated the high-tech company and stole many secrets.
Caithness was infiltrated with a palpable sense of being underimagined.

s.d: To cause to penetrate in this way.
x: The agency infiltrated several spies into the company.

s.d: To pass through something by filtration.
To invade or penetrate a tissue or organ.
x: High-grade tumors often infiltrate surrounding structures.

s.d: To send (soldiers, spies, etc.) through gaps in the enemy line.
To move from a vein, remaining in the body.

infiltration.e: From Middle English infiltracioun, from Medieval Latin infiltrātiōnem, infiltrātiō. By surface analysis, infiltrat(e) + -ion.

the slow passage of a liquid through a filtering medium

the infiltration of seawater through the lava

s.d: (uncountable) The act or process of infiltrating, as of water into a porous substance, or of a fluid into the cells of an organ or part of the body.
(uncountable) The substance which has entered the pores or cavities of a body.
x: calcareous infiltrations filling the cavities

s.d: (uncountable) The act of secretly entering a physical location and/or organization.

inflame.e: From Middle English inflammen, enflamen, enflaumen (“to set (something) on fire; to be on fire; (figurative) to enrage (someone); to become enraged; to incite (someone) to do evil; to inspire (someone); (medicine) to cause inflammation of (a body part)”), from Old French enflamer, enflammer (“to set (something) on fire, inflame; to be on fire; (figurative) to fuel (a debate, hatred, etc.)”) (modern French enflammer), from Latin inflammāre, the present active infinitive of inflammō (“to set (some

s.d: become inflamed; get sore

s.d: To set (someone or something) on fire; to cause (someone or something) to burn, flame, or glow; to kindle.
x: [Jesus, you] art the eternal Orator, vvhich both outvvardlie talkeſt to mankinde by thy Goſpel, and invvardlie in our harts inflameſt thy light vvhich is true confeſſion, faith, and comfort in thee: […]
[W]e ſhould haue made retreate, / By light of the inflamed fleet, vvith all the Greeks eſcheate; […]

s.d: To cause (something) to appear bright or red, as if on fire; to brighten, to redden.
x: I vvill my ſelf conduct thee on thy VVay, / VVhen next the Southing Sun inflames the Day; / VVhen the dry Herbage thirſts for Devvs in vain, / And Sheep, in Shades, avoid the parching Plain.
Even now we see the redness of the torches / Inflame the night to the eastward, and the clarions / Gasp (?) to us on the wind's wave.

s.d: To cause (the body or a body part) to feel abnormally or unusually hot; specifically (medicine), to cause inflammation, including abnormal heat, pain, redness, swelling, etc., in (the body or a body part).
x: to inflame the eyes by overwork
His lyver is al enflamed with drinkyng of hote wynes: […]

s.d: (figuratively) To cause (someone, or their heart, mind, etc.) to feel strong desire or other feelings; to excite (someone) to great passion; specifically, to cause (someone) to feel anger or rage; to anger, to enrage, to incense.
x: You are not VVood, you are not Stones, but men: / And being men, hearing the VVill of Cæſar, / It vvill inflame you, it vvill make you mad; […]

s.d: (figuratively) To excite or intensify (a feeling, such as an appetite or passion), especially to an excessive or unnatural level.

s.d: (figuratively) To cause (something intangible, such as a dispute or violence, or hunger or thirst) to become more serious or worse; to aggravate, to exacerbate.
x: They often drank of this stream, which had such a particular quality in it, that though it refreshed them for a time, it rather inflamed than quenched their thirst.

s.d: (figuratively, obsolete) To increase (the price or quantity of something).

x: She has been happily involved with the same woman for almost three years. During that time, they have grown together, dealt well with their problems and have worked consistently for a loving and trusting relationship.

invulnerable.e: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.

x: gunners raked the beach from invulnerable positions on the cliffs

s.d: Incapable of being injured; not vulnerable.

s.d: Unanswerable; irrefutable.

x: [T]his man is a servant of the eyes of men, and offers parchment or a white skin in sacrifice, but the flesh and the inwards he leaves to be consumed by a stranger fire.
Then sacrificing, laid the inwards and their fat.

x:
Noble and milde this Perſean ſeemes to be,
If outward habit Iudge the inward man.

(obsolete) Internal to a particular place or country; not foreign, domestic.

inwardness.e: From Middle English inwardnesse; analysable as inward + -ness.
